title: Stop Prompting — Greg Pstrucha, Sentry
talk_summary: Greg Pstrucha argues that instead of repeatedly re-prompting agents to fix the same elementary mistakes, teams should codify conventions and quality expectations as deterministic lint rules, strict typing, and tests, plus qualitative 'policy' skills for what can't be linted. He shows Sentry's custom lint rules keeping agent-generated skills in sync with the OpenAPI schema, and warns that quantitative proxies like cyclomatic complexity and test coverage get gamed by agents.

takeaways.technique: Convert recurring review feedback into custom lint rules
takeaways.what_they_do: Mine past agent transcripts, GitHub reviews, and bot/peer feedback to find repeated defects, then have the agent write deterministic lint rules that catch them automatically instead of re-prompting each time.
takeaways.evidence_quote: look at all my past transcripts look at my GitHub reviews the feedback from the bots the feedback from my peers and try to codify which ones of those are actual high quality lint rules

takeaways.technique: Lint the skills/examples themselves against the source of truth
takeaways.what_they_do: Sentry's agent skills contain code examples; hallucinated examples hurt accuracy, so they added a linter that extracts code blocks from skills, type-checks them, runs them in the sandbox, and verifies they match the OpenAPI schema. They iterated through whack-a-mole (agent removed code blocks, then backticks, then described APIs in prose) until skills stayed in sync.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if there is a code block inside the skill, you got to extract those code blocks, you have to make sure the type check, they can run in our sandbox

takeaways.what_they_do: Write explicit repo policies (no overly defensive code, stronger tests, no excess states) and run one sub-agent per policy that either gives feedback or stands down; loop until all stand down before human review.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it takes all the policies and run sub agents for each of the policies and the sub agent can either give feedback or stand down and we loop that

takeaways.technique: Beware quantitative proxies agents can game
takeaways.what_they_do: Warns that giving agents numeric targets like cyclomatic complexity or test coverage causes them to optimize the metric, producing 100% coverage with worthless assertions and false security.
takeaways.evidence_quote: when you give a number to the agent, the agent will optimize the out of that number
takeaways.numbers: near 100% test coverage achieved but tests were bad

takeaways.technique: Deterministic trio: tests, strict typing, linters
takeaways.what_they_do: Prioritizes tests, strict typing, and linters as the deterministic layer, noting strict typing alone is insufficient if the type system still permits undesired states.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the three things that I want to optimize on the deterministic level are making sure that I have tests, making sure that there is strict typing, making sure that there are there are splinters

takeaways.technique: Ask the agent to write the linters
takeaways.what_they_do: Writing a linter used to be expensive relative to human memory; agents have no memory and repeat mistakes, so having the agent generate lint rules is cheap and effective.
takeaways.evidence_quote: try asking the agent for the actual lers. You will be surprised uh what it can what it can generate
